scope: Standing preferences cover two languages, TypeScript and Rust. Rust gets the same categories as the TypeScript toolchain. Native and game options are limited to those built with TypeScript or Rust; Python, Go, Swift, Kotlin, C#, GDScript, and C++ toolchains are decided by the project that needs one.

out_of_scope.what: Categories only a product's requirements raise, such as a CMS, e-commerce, maps, rich-text editors, vector search, or model training
out_of_scope.why: no standing preference without a requirement; the architecture interview raises them when a project needs one

out_of_scope.what: Toolchains for Python, Go, Swift, Kotlin, C#, GDScript, C++, and other languages
out_of_scope.why: the user expects to build only in TypeScript and Rust; a project that needs another language decides its toolchain then

out_of_scope.what: Editor-led game engines (Godot, Unity, Unreal, Defold), code-first frameworks in C or Lua (raylib, LÖVE), native mobile and desktop UI in Swift, Kotlin, Dart, C#, or C++ (SwiftUI, Compose, Flutter, WinUI, Avalonia, Qt), and Photon's C# netcode
out_of_scope.why: their languages fall outside TypeScript and Rust; Godot's Rust bindings and Rust engines other than Bevy were not researched

out_of_scope.what: AI evaluations (Inspect AI, DeepEval, Ragas, Pydantic Evals), local model runtimes (Ollama, llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM), and AI SDKs and agent frameworks outside TypeScript (Python's, and Rust's Rig)
out_of_scope.why: the evaluation tools researched are Python-centred, and a local model runtime depends on the hardware and model a project picks; TypeScript AI is covered by `ai-sdk` and `ai-agents`

source-hosting.title: Source hosting and code review
source-hosting.decides: where repositories, pull requests, issues, and reviews live
source-hosting.why: gh and GitHub's APIs are what agents and these skills drive (basecamp issues, babysit-pr)
source-hosting.override_when: a client mandates its own forge
over: GitLab: rewriting CI and the gh-based skill flows

ci-provider.title: CI provider
ci-provider.decides: where pipelines are defined and scheduled

choices.option: GitHub Actions, with third-party actions pinned by commit SHA

ci-provider.why: follows the hosting choice; reviews and checks in one place
ci-provider.override_when: pipelines outgrow Actions, such as heavy GPU work or device farms

ci-runners.title: CI runners
ci-runners.decides: where CI jobs execute; usually decided by how heavy a project's builds are

choices.when: the repository belongs to a GitHub organisation
the project is relatively small, or the repository is personal

ci-runners.why: user choice, no reason given; the organisation and personal conditions follow from Blacksmith's organisation-only support
ci-runners.override_when: a project needs special hardware or a private network
over: larger runners: plan limits and price

toolchain-pinning.title: Toolchain and version pinning
toolchain-pinning.decides: how a project pins its language runtimes and tools so people, CI, and agents use the same versions
toolchain-pinning.why: user choice, no reason given; mise has to be installed in CI and for agents
toolchain-pinning.override_when: a host or build image reads only the ecosystem's own pin, such as `.node-version`; keep that pin in step with mise
over: the ecosystem's own pin first: the interview's recommendation
Nix and (f) devenv/Devbox: Nix's learning curve

task-runner.title: Task runner
task-runner.decides: where a project's commands, such as check, build, and dev, are defined
task-runner.why: user choice, no reason given; follows `toolchain-pinning`, with mise owning tools and tasks
task-runner.override_when: a project does not use mise; its justfile or manifest scripts then hold the commands
over: the ecosystem's own scripts first: the interview's recommendation

git-hooks.title: Git hooks
git-hooks.decides: local checks on commit or push; CI remains the real gate either way

choices.when: a project wants local gates, such as several humans committing

git-hooks.why: agents commit often; hooks slow every commit or get bypassed, and the full check already runs before handoff
git-hooks.override_when: several humans commit and want local feedback

agent-hooks.title: Agent hooks
agent-hooks.decides: harness hooks around agent actions; each harness (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Grok) needs its own
agent-hooks.why: skills such as implement-outline already run the full check before finishing, and every harness would need its own hook
agent-hooks.override_when: agents often hand back unformatted or failing code; then a stop hook that runs format and lint
over: stop hook: one setup per harness

secret-scanning.title: Secret scanning
secret-scanning.decides: catching leaked credentials before and after a push; server-side and CI scanning combine
secret-scanning.why: user choice of order, no reason given; both run together as recommended
secret-scanning.override_when: push protection is unavailable on a private repository's plan; Betterleaks then runs alone

dependency-updates.title: Dependency updates
dependency-updates.decides: automated pull requests that keep dependencies current; a planned dependency-update skill will also cover upstream-source references
dependency-updates.why: grouped, scheduled update PRs suit review by agents and people
dependency-updates.override_when: a repository only needs GitHub Actions updates

vulnerability-scanning.title: Vulnerability scanning
vulnerability-scanning.decides: detecting known-vulnerable dependencies; separate from update bots

choices.when: on a schedule, for what is merged

vulnerability-scanning.why: one gate at review plus one sweep across ecosystems
vulnerability-scanning.override_when: the plan lacks dependency review on a private repository; OSV-Scanner then also runs on pull requests
over: package-manager audit: one tool per ecosystem

local-container-runtime.title: Local container runtime
local-container-runtime.decides: what projects may assume is installed to run local services
local-container-runtime.why: no daemon first, as recommended; Docker Desktop second is user choice, no reason given
local-container-runtime.override_when: a client's environment requires another runtime
over: OrbStack: the interview's recommendation if licensed

local-services.title: Local services
local-services.decides: how one command starts the whole system locally

choices.option: Embedded stores plus the dev task

choices.when: a store has no embedded form

local-services.why: one command with no container daemon keeps local runs and checks fast for people and agents
local-services.override_when: a service exists only as a container image
over: Overmind: another tool beside the dev task

devcontainer.title: Devcontainer recipe
devcontainer.decides: whether projects ship a repository-defined development container
devcontainer.why: a container earns its upkeep only when native setup is hard
devcontainer.override_when: a team needs one identical environment for everyone; then every project ships one

commits-and-branches.title: Commits and branches
commits-and-branches.decides: branch lifetime, merge style, and commit messages

choices.option: Short-lived branches, squash merge, conventional PR title

commits-and-branches.why: agent-made branches stay cheap while main stays semantic for release tooling
commits-and-branches.override_when: a project's release tooling needs every commit to be conventional
over: keep conventional commits: hygiene on every branch
trunk-based: release tooling cannot parse history

release.title: Release and versioning
release.decides: how a project versions and publishes releases, which differs per project
release.decided_by: what the project distributes and to whom
over: dist/GoReleaser: native binaries, revisited with Rust

agent-isolation.title: Agent isolation
agent-isolation.why: T3 already gives each agent its own worktree; a sandbox only when the code itself is untrusted
agent-isolation.override_when: agents must run code from untrusted sources
over: devcontainer with scoped mounts: only as tight as its mounts

dev-secrets.title: Development secrets
dev-secrets.decides: how secrets reach local runs and CI without plaintext in the repository

choices.when: a throwaway project, or the free plan's projects run out

dev-secrets.why: no plaintext on disk and no keys to manage, and per-project machine accounts keep an agent's token to one project's secrets
dev-secrets.override_when: a client or team keeps its secrets in another manager
over: Bitwarden CLI: an unlocked session exposes the whole vault

js-runtime.title: JavaScript runtime
js-runtime.decides: where TypeScript runs in production and for tools
js-runtime.why: LTS and compatibility for production; Bun's startup and single-file binaries for tools
js-runtime.override_when: a host or framework requires another runtime

package-manager.title: Package manager
package-manager.why: pnpm's strict layout catches undeclared imports agents add
package-manager.override_when: a host or framework requires another manager

monorepo.title: Monorepo orchestration
monorepo.decides: task ordering and caching across workspace packages
monorepo.why: user choice, no reason given; Turborepo first at any size
monorepo.override_when: a repository has a single package
over: plain workspaces for two or three packages: the interview's recommendation's second, kept here only under Bun

formatter.title: Formatter
formatter.decides: mechanical formatting for code and common file types
formatter.why: user choice for the second, no reason given; oxfmt first as recommended
formatter.override_when: until `bun fmt` is in a stable release, Bun projects keep oxfmt
revisit_when: `bun fmt` ships in a stable Bun release

linter.title: Linter and rule policy
linter.decides: static rules, type-aware checks, and custom policy
linter.why: fast type-aware feedback on agent-typical mistakes; the Bun choice is user choice, no reason given
linter.override_when: until `bun lint` is in a stable release and runs anti-slop's rules, Bun projects keep Oxlint
revisit_when: `bun lint` ships in a stable Bun release and runs anti-slop's rules

type-checker.title: Type checker
type-checker.why: the native compiler is stable and much faster; framework checkers only where components need them
type-checker.override_when: a tool the project needs depends on the pre-7 compiler API

strictness.title: TypeScript strictness
strictness.decides: which compile-time checks every project promises

choices.option: `strict` plus `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noImplicitOverride`, `noImplicitReturns`, `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch`, and `noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature`; unused code left to the linter and analyzer

strictness.why: the compiler catches silent mistakes before review
strictness.override_when: generated code or a library's types make a flag impractical; relax it for those files only, with the reason beside the setting
over: strict plus precise access: fewer checks

code-hygiene.title: Code hygiene, duplication, and complexity
code-hygiene.decides: repository-wide unused code, unused dependencies, clones, and complexity

choices.option: fallow, blocking in the full check

code-hygiene.why: one tool covers every hygiene scope, and blocking keeps it from turning advisory
code-hygiene.override_when: a project fallow cannot analyse, such as one built mainly in another language

architecture-boundaries.title: Architecture boundaries
architecture-boundaries.decides: enforcing which packages and layers may import which
architecture-boundaries.why: fallow first as recommended, adding no tool; the later order is user choice, no reason given

unit-tests.title: Unit and integration test runner
unit-tests.decides: local test execution, isolation, and coverage

choices.when: packages that run only on Bun

unit-tests.why: the same tests run on Node, in a real browser, and in the Workers pool, and Effect's test helpers need Vitest
unit-tests.override_when: a package runs only on Bun

browser-tests.title: End-to-end and browser testing
browser-tests.decides: real-browser product journeys and browser component checks
browser-tests.why: Playwright is what agents and computer-use tooling already drive
browser-tests.override_when: a product runs outside a browser

app-build.title: Application build
app-build.decides: dev server and production bundles, unless a meta-framework owns them

choices.when: the meta-framework does not own the build

app-build.why: every framework preferred here builds on Vite; Bun's bundler second is user choice, no reason given

library-build.title: Library build
library-build.decides: building packages others import: formats, declarations, exports

choices.when: bundling or dual formats are needed

library-build.why: most packages need only compiled ESM and declarations
library-build.override_when: a package must ship CommonJS or bundled assets

effect.title: Effect or plain TypeScript
effect.decides: how code handles errors, concurrency, dependencies, and resources
effect.override_when: a library whose consumers must not take on Effect, or code where breaking changes in Effect's unstable modules are unacceptable
over: plain TypeScript for UI code, small tools, and libraries others consume: the interview's recommendation's second
revisit_when: Effect declares its unstable modules stable: schema, http, http-api, ai, sql, workflow, cli

frontend-framework.title: Frontend framework
frontend-framework.decides: the UI component and rendering model for web products
frontend-framework.why: agents are most fluent in React, and the libraries chosen here target it first; Svelte second is user choice, no reason given
frontend-framework.override_when: a project's ecosystem or team is built on another framework

meta-framework.title: Meta-framework
meta-framework.decides: routing, rendering, and server integration around the UI framework
meta-framework.why: TanStack Start first as recommended (Vite build, typed end to end, Node or Workers hosting); the rest of the order is user choice, no reason given
meta-framework.override_when: a project's shape favours a lighter option, such as a content site (Astro) or a static internal tool behind an API (Vite SPA); SvelteKit applies only with Svelte

styling.title: Styling
styling.why: user choice, no reason given; StyleX is what Astryx (`ui-components`) is authored in
styling.override_when: a component library or template the project adopts assumes Tailwind

ui-components.title: UI components
ui-components.decides: which components a project owns, themes, or consumes

choices.when: a brand needs its own component system built from primitives

ui-components.why: user choice, no reason given; Astryx themes through CSS custom properties, so a brand kit's tokens can drive it
ui-components.override_when: a project cannot take on a design system in beta, or does not run React 19

server-state.title: Server state
server-state.decides: loading, caching, and invalidating remote data in the client

choices.option: TanStack Query, with router loaders prefetching into it

server-state.why: the caching, invalidation, and mutations an interactive app needs, without request waterfalls
server-state.override_when: data loads only on navigation and never refetches

client-state.title: Client state
client-state.decides: interaction state that is not server data

choices.when: state is shared across distant components

client-state.why: most state belongs in components or the URL; Effect Atom fourth is user choice, no reason given
client-state.override_when: a framework other than React, where its own reactivity applies

runtime-schemas.title: Runtime schemas
runtime-schemas.decides: validating untrusted input and deriving types from it
runtime-schemas.why: follows `effect`: one schema system across Effect code, its HTTP API, and RPC
runtime-schemas.override_when: a breaking change in Effect's unstable `schema` module is unacceptable for the project

forms.title: Forms
forms.why: typed fields validated with the same schemas as the server
forms.override_when: a framework other than React, with its own form tooling

api-style.title: API style
api-style.decides: the contract between clients and the server

choices.when: one full-stack app is the only client
a CLI, mobile app, other service, or the public calls the API

api-style.why: follows `effect`; tRPC third is user choice, no reason given
api-style.override_when: a codebase built without Effect, where tRPC fits

backend-framework.title: Backend framework
backend-framework.decides: the HTTP server for services outside the meta-framework

choices.when: the app's own server covers the product

backend-framework.why: no second server until something needs one, and Effect when it does; the later order is user choice, no reason given

primary-database.title: Primary database

choices.when: local-first, single-host, self-hosted, or on Cloudflare

primary-database.why: Postgres serves multi-user products on any host, and SQLite removes the server where one writer is enough; Convex third is user choice, no reason given
primary-database.override_when: a product built around reactive sync, where Convex's platform fits first

orm.title: ORM and migrations
orm.why: typed, SQL-shaped queries and migrations across Postgres, SQLite, and D1; Effect SQL second is user choice, no reason given
orm.override_when: Effect's `sql` module becomes stable in an Effect-first codebase

caching.title: Caching and shared state
caching.decides: cross-process caches, rate limits, and short-lived shared state
caching.why: most apps need no shared cache; the platform's own storage before running a server
caching.override_when: several instances must share state from the start

auth.title: Authentication

choices.when: enterprise SSO or directory sync is a requirement

auth.why: users and sessions stay in the project's database; Clerk third is user choice, no reason given
auth.override_when: enterprise SSO or directory sync is required from the start

payments.title: Payments
payments.decides: taking money, and who is the merchant of record
payments.why: user choice, no reason given; as merchant of record Polar takes on international sales tax and needs only Stripe Connect Express payouts in the merchant's country
payments.override_when: the merchant's country is not on Polar's payout list (Iraq is not), or the product is not eligible for a merchant of record
over: Stripe first: the interview's recommendation, speculative

email.title: Transactional email
email.why: a TypeScript-first API with templates written as React components
email.override_when: the client already sends through another provider

background-jobs.title: Background jobs and workflows
background-jobs.decides: deferred work, retries, schedules, and durable execution
background-jobs.why: durable work runs on the platform already hosting the app; the later order is user choice, no reason given
background-jobs.override_when: a business process needs Temporal-grade durability across services

realtime.title: Realtime
realtime.why: most live updates are one-way; rooms on the project's own Cloudflare account before a service
realtime.override_when: the host is not Cloudflare and rooms are needed

file-storage.title: File storage
file-storage.why: S3-compatible storage bound directly to Workers
file-storage.override_when: the project is hosted on AWS

search.title: Search
search.why: no second system to keep in sync
search.override_when: search is the product's core feature

frontend-hosting.title: Frontend hosting
frontend-hosting.decides: where web apps and sites are served

choices.when: a Next.js app needs features Cloudflare's adapter lacks

frontend-hosting.why: one platform for apps, storage, queues, and databases

backend-hosting.title: Backend hosting
backend-hosting.decides: where services and long-lived processes run
backend-hosting.why: Workers first as recommended; the rest of the order is user choice, no reason given
backend-hosting.override_when: a service needs long-lived processes or native binaries, which Workers rule out; the next choice applies

database-hosting.title: Database hosting
database-hosting.why: a database branch per preview for Postgres, and D1 bound directly to Workers
database-hosting.override_when: data residency requires a region the host does not offer

infrastructure-as-code.title: Infrastructure as code
infrastructure-as-code.why: user choice, no reason given; Alchemy is TypeScript on Effect (`effect`)
infrastructure-as-code.override_when: a project needs a stable release (Alchemy's latest is a beta)
over: platform configuration first: the interview's recommendation

observability.title: Observability
observability.decides: errors, traces, and logs in production
observability.why: Sentry groups errors and traces with source maps in minutes
observability.override_when: a client requires its own telemetry platform

product-analytics.title: Product analytics
product-analytics.why: events, funnels, replays, and flags in one tool for products
product-analytics.override_when: a client's marketing team requires its own analytics

feature-flags.title: Feature flags

choices.when: a rollout or experiment needs targeting

feature-flags.why: flags are worth a service only once targeting is needed
feature-flags.override_when: a product runs experiments from launch

i18n.title: Internationalisation
i18n.why: typed message keys catch missing translations at compile time
i18n.override_when: a framework or translation workflow requires another library

ai-sdk.title: AI SDK
ai-sdk.decides: model calls, streaming, tools, and structured output
ai-sdk.why: stable across providers, where Effect AI is still unstable
ai-sdk.override_when: Effect's `ai` module becomes stable in an Effect-first codebase

ai-agents.title: AI agents
ai-agents.decides: agent loops, tools, and handoffs inside a product
ai-agents.why: an in-app agent runs in the same SDK as its model calls; the later order is user choice, no reason given
ai-agents.override_when: the agent works on files, a shell, and code

docs-site.title: Documentation sites
docs-site.why: Starlight stays in TypeScript and Astro with search built in; mdBook for Rust books
docs-site.override_when: a project's docs live in another site generator already
over: Material for MkDocs: end of life

rust-toolchain.title: Rust toolchain pinning
rust-toolchain.decides: how a Rust project pins its compiler, components, and targets, beside mise for everything else (`toolchain-pinning`)

choices.option: `rust-toolchain.toml`, with mise installing everything else and leaving the Rust version to the file

rust-toolchain.why: every Rust tool, editor, and CI action reads it, and it holds the components and targets
rust-toolchain.override_when: a project builds entirely through Nix

rust-lint-policy.title: Rust lint policy
rust-lint-policy.decides: how strict rustfmt, Clippy, and the compiler are; the Rust counterpart of `linter` and `strictness`

choices.option: Clippy's `pedantic` group with each allowed lint and its reason in `[workspace.lints]`, rustfmt defaults, warnings denied through `build.warnings`

rust-lint-policy.why: Clippy catches what agents get wrong silently, as strict TypeScript does in `strictness`
rust-lint-policy.override_when: generated code or FFI bindings; allow lints for those modules only, with reasons

rust-dependency-hygiene.title: Rust dependency hygiene
rust-dependency-hygiene.decides: advisories, licences, sources, and unused dependencies; the Rust counterpart of `code-hygiene`

choices.option: cargo-machete, both in the full check

rust-dependency-hygiene.why: one policy for advisories, licences, and sources, plus an unused-dependency check fast enough for every run
rust-dependency-hygiene.override_when: cargo-machete misreports a crate used only through macros; record the exception beside its setting

rust-tests.title: Rust tests
rust-tests.decides: running tests, and the test techniques beside them; the Rust counterpart of `unit-tests`
rust-tests.why: nextest keeps large suites fast; snapshots and properties supplement it

rust-async.title: Rust async runtime
rust-async.decides: whether and how Rust code runs asynchronously; the role Effect plays in TypeScript

choices.when: a tool has no concurrent I/O

rust-async.why: the crates a Rust service needs assume Tokio

rust-web-framework.title: Rust web framework
rust-web-framework.decides: HTTP services written in Rust, when a project needs one rather than a TypeScript backend (`backend-framework`)
rust-web-framework.why: Axum composes with Tokio and Tower; Actix Web second is user choice, no reason given
rust-web-framework.override_when: a TypeScript backend (`backend-framework`) serves the need, which is the usual case

rust-cli-args.title: Rust CLI arguments
rust-cli-args.decides: flags, subcommands, help, and completions for Rust CLIs
rust-cli-args.why: clap's derive API reads like the CLI it builds, and agents reach for it
rust-cli-args.override_when: a tiny binary where clap's size matters

rust-errors.title: Rust error handling
rust-errors.why: the standard pairing across the ecosystem
rust-errors.override_when: errors need rich context across many layers

rust-serialization.title: Rust serialization
rust-serialization.why: one derive covers JSON, TOML, and most formats

rust-tui.title: Rust terminal UIs
rust-tui.why: Ratatui is the maintained full-screen library
rust-tui.override_when: a form-heavy tool, where a widget toolkit fits

rust-library-publishing.title: Rust library publishing
rust-library-publishing.decides: where Rust libraries are published and their API docs hosted
rust-library-publishing.why: public crates get docs.rs for free; cargo-semver-checks and cargo-hack guard compatibility
rust-library-publishing.override_when: private crates shared across many projects

rust-binary-distribution.title: Rust binary distribution
rust-binary-distribution.decides: how people install a Rust CLI

choices.option: GitHub release binaries built by dist

rust-binary-distribution.override_when: the audience are Rust developers, where `cargo install` suffices

ts-cli-framework.title: TypeScript CLI framework
ts-cli-framework.decides: commands, arguments, validation, help, and completions for TypeScript CLIs

choices.when: the tool is built on Effect

ts-cli-framework.why: an Effect tool parses its arguments into the same typed services and errors; Commander is what agents know best elsewhere
ts-cli-framework.override_when: a breaking change in Effect's unstable `cli` module is unacceptable for the tool

ts-tui.title: TypeScript terminal UIs and prompts
ts-tui.decides: prompts and full-screen terminal apps in TypeScript

choices.when: rendering speed matters and the tool is a full app

ts-tui.why: Clack is stable and polished for guided flows; OpenTUI's condition and Ink third are user choice, no reason given
ts-tui.override_when: the tool must run on Node 24, below OpenTUI's Node 26.4 floor

ts-cli-distribution.title: TypeScript CLI distribution
ts-cli-distribution.decides: what users install to run a TypeScript tool

choices.when: users should not need a runtime

ts-cli-distribution.why: developers already have a runtime, and trusted publishing removes long-lived tokens
ts-cli-distribution.override_when: a private package, which publishes through OIDC without provenance

rust-in-typescript.title: Rust inside TypeScript projects
rust-in-typescript.decides: how Rust code reaches a TypeScript app or tool

choices.option: Rust binary through npm platform packages
choices.when: a CLI engine, or the host runs on Bun
it must run in a browser

rust-in-typescript.why: a subprocess works under Node and Bun alike, while addons on Bun are best effort
rust-in-typescript.override_when: the boundary is crossed so often that process calls are too slow

rust-database.title: Rust database access
rust-database.decides: SQL access and migrations for Rust services and tools

choices.when: embedded SQLite in a synchronous tool

rust-database.why: SQL-shaped and compile-checked, like Drizzle; when TypeScript shares the database, Drizzle Kit (`orm`) owns migrations
rust-database.override_when: a domain model needs an ORM's relations

rust-observability.title: Rust observability
rust-observability.decides: diagnostics, traces, and error reports from Rust
rust-observability.why: one instrumentation layer feeding Sentry, as the web stack does in `observability`
rust-observability.override_when: a tiny synchronous tool, where `log` with `env_logger` is enough

rust-cross-compilation.title: Rust cross-compilation
rust-cross-compilation.decides: building Rust binaries for each platform

choices.option: GitHub Actions native matrix, driven by dist

choices.when: a Linux glibc baseline or one build host

rust-cross-compilation.why: native runners build each target where it runs, and dist writes that workflow
rust-cross-compilation.override_when: a target with no hosted runner

rust-cli-tests.title: Rust CLI integration tests
rust-cli-tests.decides: testing a Rust CLI as a process
rust-cli-tests.why: precise exit-code and output checks; trycmd scales to many cases
rust-cli-tests.override_when: a full-screen terminal app, which needs PTY tests

mixed-repositories.title: Mixed TypeScript and Rust repositories
mixed-repositories.decides: running tasks across both languages in one repository

choices.option: Cargo workspace beside the pnpm workspace, with mise tasks running both

revisit_when: Turborepo's Cargo workspace support leaves experimental

scripts.title: Single-file scripts
scripts.decides: small automations run without a project scaffold

choices.when: Rust crates or speed are needed

scripts.override_when: a script needs a sandbox with explicit permissions

quick-ui.title: Quick UIs for one-off tools
quick-ui.decides: the smallest interface for a utility
quick-ui.why: a single file opens anywhere; the terminal UI third is user choice, no reason given
quick-ui.override_when: the tool must read local files or run unattended

mobile-client-state.title: Mobile client state
mobile-client-state.decides: interaction state in a mobile app that is not server data

choices.when: state is shared across distant components

mobile-client-state.override_when: a mobile approach other than React Native is chosen (`mobile-approach`)

mobile-server-state.title: Mobile server state
mobile-server-state.decides: loading, caching, and invalidating remote data in a mobile app

choices.option: TanStack Query, wired to React Native's connectivity and app-focus events

mobile-server-state.override_when: a mobile approach other than React Native is chosen (`mobile-approach`)

mobile-approach.title: Mobile approach
mobile-approach.decides: how a mobile app is built

choices.when: an installable web app is enough

mobile-approach.why: keeps TypeScript and React, with builds and updates as services
mobile-approach.override_when: deep platform integration a React Native module cannot reach

mobile-navigation.title: Mobile navigation
mobile-navigation.decides: screens, deep links, and routes in an Expo app
mobile-navigation.why: file routes with deep links by default

mobile-styling.title: Mobile styling
mobile-styling.decides: styling native views; web CSS, including StyleX (`styling`), does not style them
mobile-styling.why: typed themes from brand tokens on the StyleSheet API
mobile-styling.override_when: a shared native and web design system, where Tamagui fits

mobile-storage.title: Mobile local storage
mobile-storage.decides: on-device data that is not secret

mobile-offline-sync.title: Mobile offline sync
mobile-offline-sync.decides: local writes and server changes converging across devices
mobile-offline-sync.decided_by: the conflict rules the product needs
mobile-offline-sync.why: conflict rules differ per product; PowerSync fits the Postgres preference

mobile-secrets.title: Mobile secret storage
mobile-secrets.decides: tokens and credentials on the device
mobile-secrets.why: one API over Keychain and Keystore

mobile-tests.title: Mobile tests

choices.option: Jest with jest-expo and RN Testing Library

mobile-tests.why: Expo's documented test path, plus simple device flows

mobile-builds.title: Mobile builds and store submission
mobile-builds.decides: building, signing, and submitting store binaries

choices.when: the pipeline must stay in GitHub Actions

mobile-builds.why: no macOS build machine to own
mobile-builds.override_when: a client requires builds inside its own CI

mobile-ota.title: Over-the-air updates
mobile-ota.decides: shipping JavaScript changes between store releases
mobile-ota.why: channels and rollback without running delivery

desktop-runtime.title: Desktop runtime
desktop-runtime.decides: how a TypeScript interface becomes a desktop app

choices.when: one consistent browser engine or Node APIs are required

desktop-runtime.why: TypeScript for the interface and Rust for the host
desktop-runtime.override_when: web-view differences across operating systems break the product

desktop-packaging.title: Desktop packaging, updates, and signing
desktop-packaging.decides: packaging, auto-updates, and code signing for direct distribution
desktop-packaging.override_when: store distribution, which uses the store's updates

app-crash-reporting.title: Crash and error reporting for apps
app-crash-reporting.decides: crashes and errors from mobile and desktop apps
app-crash-reporting.why: one service across web, mobile, desktop, and Rust
app-crash-reporting.override_when: a client requires another crash service

app-analytics.title: App and game analytics
app-analytics.decides: usage and player analytics outside the web
app-analytics.why: the same tool as `product-analytics` for apps; player metrics for games
app-analytics.override_when: a client's analytics platform is mandated

in-app-purchases.title: In-app purchases
in-app-purchases.why: Apple and Google billing without building an entitlement backend
in-app-purchases.override_when: a single store with simple purchases

push.title: Push notifications
push.why: one send API for both platforms

game-tests.title: Game tests
game-tests.decides: testing game logic and rendered behaviour

choices.option: Vitest for logic and Playwright for rendered and input checks

game-tests.override_when: an engine with its own test runner

game-engine.title: Game engine
game-engine.decides: the engine for a game, in TypeScript or Rust
game-engine.why: full engines rather than renderers to build an engine around
game-engine.override_when: a game needing an editor-led engine

web-game-toolchain.title: Web game toolchain
web-game-toolchain.decides: how a web game is authored and built

choices.option: TypeScript, Vite, and the engine package

web-game-toolchain.override_when: a scene-heavy game, where an editor helps

game-assets.title: Game asset version control
game-assets.decides: versioning code and large binary assets
game-assets.why: nothing new until assets are large
game-assets.override_when: artists work on large binary datasets

game-distribution.title: Game distribution
game-distribution.why: each channel for its kind of release
game-distribution.override_when: a mobile game, which goes through the stores

multiplayer.title: Multiplayer backend

choices.when: accounts and social features are needed

multiplayer.why: rooms on the platform the project already hosts on
multiplayer.override_when: competitive real-time games needing managed server fleets
